title: Teach one
hookLine: convey from me, even one verse (Bukhari), with the warning against lying about the Prophet in the same breath
tomorrow: forty sayings, done. so what are the ninety-nine?

cards: A quote with the Prophet's name on it drifts by on a pastel background, shared and reshared. Nobody in the comments asks where it's from. Yesterday's question was who gets to pass a hadith on.
Sahih al-Bukhari has a report that answers it, and the answer pulls two ways in a single breath.

teach.h: CONVEY FROM ME, EVEN ONE VERSE.
teach.b: In paraphrase: convey from me, even if it's one verse. Tell stories from the Children of Israel; there's no harm in it. And whoever lies about me on purpose, let him take his seat in the Fire.
Both halves sit in the same hadith, and two views inside the tradition each lean on one.

teach.h: PASS IT ON: THE BAR IS ONE.
teach.b: The first says: pass it on. Even one verse. The hadith sets the bar at one, not at a degree.
A grandmother at the stove counts. If only experts speak, plenty of homes go quiet, and the very words of the hadith ask for more voices, not fewer.

teach.h: CAREFUL: THE WARNING IS RIGHT THERE.
teach.b: The second says: careful. The hardest warning about the Prophet's words is in that same sentence.

Scholars spent lifetimes checking chains because a false report travels as fast as a true one, and a confident mistake can outrun a correct whisper. So leave the teaching to people trained in the sources.

teach.h: SURE OF IT, SOURCED, NO RULINGS.
teach.b: Scholars have held the two together like this: pass on what you're sure of, say where it comes from, and leave rulings to those trained to give them.
Something to tell a friend tonight: the hadith telling ordinary people to teach is the same one warning them not to make things up.

how: Muslims often share a short hadith with family or friends, naming its collection; questions of law are taken to scholars trained to answer them.

practice: Choose the one you memorized yesterday, or any of the forty you're sure of. Text it to one person who'd like it, in a sentence or two, with where it's from: al-Nawawi's forty, and its number.
For the sit, put the phone face down and let it go.

wordCard.voice: Teach one: pass on a single hadith you're sure of, and say where it comes from.

orig.note: Arabic: convey from me, even if it's one verse. the opening of the hadith in Sahih al-Bukhari.

carryVoice: The line for today: pass one on, with its source attached. That closes al-Nawawi's forty.

sources.ref: Sahih al-Bukhari 3461 (Abdullah ibn Amr: convey from me even if it is one verse; tell of the Children of Israel, there is no harm; whoever lies about me deliberately, let him take his seat in the Fire)
